name: The gospels compared, and how the New Testament came together
source: C. J. Cornthwaite, two videos on his YouTube channel: “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”, and on how the New Testament came together
licence: Arguments restated in the site’s own words; scripture quoted from the ESV
note: Commentary written for this site; the source of the arguments is named on the Sources page.

entries.title: His family said he was out of his mind: Mark 3:21
entries.content:
Mark tells of a crowd so large that Jesus and his followers could not eat. His family hears of it and sets out to take hold of him, because people are saying he has lost his mind. Ten verses later his mother and brothers arrive and stand outside, and Jesus names those around him as his true family.

And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.”

Mark 3:21

And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you.” And he answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.”

Mark 3:31-35

Matthew and Luke both copy the scene of the family standing outside. Both leave out the verse that says why the family came. A reader of Matthew or Luke meets a family that simply wants to see him.

While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. But he replied to the man who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”

Matthew 12:46-50

The omission matters because Matthew and Luke each open with a birth story in which Mary is told by an angel who her son is. A mother who had heard that could hardly set out to restrain him as a madman. Mark has no birth story, so the scene caused him no difficulty. The later writers met it in their source and removed it.

The difference is a deliberate correction of one gospel by another, made by a writer who had Mark open in front of him.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”. See Sources.

entries.title: Could not, or did not? Mark 6:5 and Matthew 13:58
entries.content:
In his home town Jesus meets disbelief. Mark says plainly that he was unable to do any mighty work there, apart from healing a few sick people. The Greek is ouk edynato, “he was not able”.

And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.

Mark 6:5-6

Matthew copies the scene and changes the sentence. Jesus now chooses not to do many mighty works there, and the reason given is their unbelief.

And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.

Matthew 13:58

A few words turn a Jesus whose power had limits into a Jesus who holds his power back. Matthew makes the same kind of change elsewhere: Mark has Jesus ask, “Why do you call me good?” (Mark 10:18), and Matthew turns it into “Why do you ask me about what is good?” (Matthew 19:17). Corrections like these are most of what readers call contradictions between the gospels. The later writer is smoothing what his source said.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”. See Sources.

entries.title: One baptism, four tellings: Mark 1:9-11
entries.content:
Mark tells it simply. Jesus comes from Nazareth and John baptises him in the Jordan. Then the heavens open, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice speaks.

In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. And a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.”

Mark 1:9-11

A baptism for the forgiveness of sins, given by John to Jesus, made later writers uneasy. Most scholars take the event as historical for that very reason: no one would invent it. Each later gospel deals with it in its own way.

Matthew adds a conversation in which John objects that Jesus should baptise him, and Jesus has to persuade him.

John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented.

Matthew 3:14-15

Luke puts John in prison before he mentions the baptism at all, and then refers to it in passing, without saying who baptised Jesus.

added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,

Luke 3:20-21

John’s gospel never tells of the baptism. John the Baptist appears as a witness who saw the Spirit come down on Jesus, and that is all.

And John bore witness: “I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ‘He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’ And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.”

John 1:32-34

Four tellings, each shaped to its writer’s theology, and each a step further from the plain event in Mark.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”. See Sources.

entries.title: Galilee or Jerusalem? Mark 16:7
entries.content:
At the empty tomb in Mark, a young man tells the women that Jesus is going ahead of the disciples to Galilee, and that they will see him there.

But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.”

Mark 16:7

Matthew follows this. The eleven go to a mountain in Galilee and see Jesus there, though some doubted.

Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted.

Matthew 28:16-17

Luke tells a different story. Every appearance happens in or near Jerusalem, and Jesus tells the disciples to stay in the city. In Acts, the same author has him order them not to leave Jerusalem, and the movement spreads outward from there.

And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

Luke 24:49

And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me;

Acts 1:4

The two accounts cannot both be right about where the risen Jesus met his followers. The difference follows each writer’s purpose. For Luke, the church must come out of Jerusalem. For Matthew, the story ends in Galilee, where it began.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”. See Sources.

entries.title: Where Lazarus came from: John 11:1-2
entries.content:
John introduces Lazarus as the brother of Mary and Martha, and tells how Jesus raised him after four days in the tomb. It is the greatest sign in the gospel, and the one that leads the authorities to plan Jesus’ death.

Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.

John 11:1-2

Mary and Martha come from Luke, where they appear in one short scene: Martha busy serving, Mary sitting at Jesus’ feet. Luke says nothing of a brother. A raising from the dead in their own house would have been worth one sentence.

Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his teaching.

Luke 10:38-39

Luke does have a Lazarus, in a parable. A poor man of that name dies and is carried to Abraham’s side, while a rich man suffers in Hades and begs that someone be sent back to warn his brothers. Abraham answers that they would not believe even if someone rose from the dead.

He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’”

Luke 16:31

John’s story reads like that parable come true. A man named Lazarus rises from the dead, and still the leaders do not believe. John appears to build a new narrative out of names and themes found in Luke. That makes the raising of Lazarus a piece of theological writing, and a weak witness to a remembered event.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”. See Sources.

entries.title: The temple at the start, or at the end? John 2:13-17
entries.content:
In Mark, Matthew and Luke, Jesus drives the traders out of the temple in his last week. Mark makes it the act that sets the chief priests looking for a way to kill him.

And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching.

Mark 11:15-18

John moves the scene to the beginning of the ministry, two chapters in, years before the end. In its place, the act that turns the authorities against Jesus is the raising of Lazarus.

The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there. And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.

John 2:13-15

Harmonisers sometimes say that Jesus cleared the temple twice. No gospel says so. John rewrites the order of the story to serve his own account of who Jesus was and why he died.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”. See Sources.

entries.title: Why there are four gospels, and why they were once one: Luke 1:1-4
entries.content:
Luke opens by saying that many had already written accounts, and that he has decided to write an orderly one of his own. A writer who thought the earlier accounts sufficient would not have needed to start again.

Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,

Luke 1:1-3

The church of the second century knew that its gospels disagreed, and it tried two answers.

One gospel made of four

Tatian, a student of Justin Martyr, wove the four into a single continuous story around the year 170. It later became known as the Diatessaron, “through the four”. For centuries it was the gospel read in the Syriac-speaking churches. A Latin harmony of the same kind opens the New Testament of the sixth-century Codex Fuldensis, in place of the four separate gospels. Justin himself may already have read from a harmony.

Four gospels, like four winds

Irenaeus, writing about 180, argued that there could be neither more nor fewer than four gospels, because there are four regions of the world and four principal winds (Against Heresies 3.11.8). The four became four views of one truth. That reasoning carried the day, and it is the root of the modern habit of laying the gospels side by side and fitting them together.

Taken to its end, the habit produces a Jesus who healed one blind man leaving Jericho and two more on the way out (Mark 10:46; Matthew 20:30). Each gospel writer seems to have written for readers who would never see the others. Read one at a time, each shows its own Jesus and its own aims, and the differences are the evidence of those aims.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, “Christians struggle to harmonize the gospels. But the contradictions are deliberate.”. See Sources.

entries.title: How the New Testament came together
themes: How the New Testament came together
entries.content:
Second Peter speaks of Paul’s letters as hard to understand, and sets them beside “the other Scriptures”. It is one of the first signs of Christian writings being read as scripture. The road from there to a fixed list of twenty-seven books took centuries, and for some churches it never ended.

And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.

2 Peter 3:15-16

Letters, then sayings

The earliest Christian writings are letters: Paul’s, from the 50s. Their mark is the claim that gentiles belong to Israel’s God as gentiles, without becoming Jews. Alongside them came writings that tell little of Jesus’ life, such as James and Revelation.

Next came collections of Jesus’ sayings. The Gospel of Thomas, a list of sayings with no story, survives whole in a Coptic copy of the fourth century and in Greek fragments from Oxyrhynchus a century or two older. Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth around 96, quotes “the words of the Lord Jesus” in a form found in no gospel (1 Clement 13). The Didache does the same. Sayings were being passed on, and written down, before and beside the gospels.

The gospels

Then sayings were set into stories. Scholars date the four gospels between about 70 and 110. Nobody names them for decades. Papias, early in the second century, says that Mark wrote down what Peter remembered, and defends him for writing “not in order”. Only fragments of Papias survive, quoted by Eusebius two centuries later (Church History 3.39). In the 150s Justin Martyr calls the gospels “memoirs of the apostles”. He never clearly quotes John. The first known commentary on John was written by Heracleon, a follower of Valentinus, whom later writers counted among the heretics.

A flood of books

The second century brought an outpouring of Christian writing: the Gospel of Peter, the Acts of Paul and Thecla, the works later found at Nag Hammadi in 1945, and many more. Their writers all claimed the apostles as their own. The labels of orthodox and heretic were drawn up afterwards, by writers such as Irenaeus and Tertullian, and fixed in the third and fourth centuries.

Most critical scholars hold that 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus belong here as well, written in Paul’s name after his death to settle the churches into ordered households while they waited for a return that had not come.

The first collection

The first person known to have gathered a Christian scripture apart from the Jewish one was Marcion of Sinope, a wealthy shipowner who came to Rome around 140. His scripture was one gospel, close to Luke, and ten letters of Paul. His opponents said he cut out what he disliked. Some scholars now argue that his gospel came first and our Luke is a reworking of it. Either way, collections were edited as they were made.

The book form made collections possible. Papyrus 46, from about 200, binds Paul’s letters into one codex with numbered pages; Papyrus 45 holds the four gospels and Acts. No early collection holds the whole New Testament as we know it.

The text itself kept changing as it was copied. Of the five thousand and more Greek manuscripts, most are from the ninth century or later; the early ones show a text still being altered, sometimes by accident and sometimes on purpose. The site’s Manuscripts pages show this passage by passage, including Luke 3:22 and 1 Timothy 3:16.

Lists and quarrels

The Muratorian Fragment, a Latin list usually dated to the late second century, accepts most of our books but lacks Hebrews, James and 1 and 2 Peter. It includes the Wisdom of Solomon and, with doubts, the Apocalypse of Peter. It also tells a story of how John came to write, which suggests that John’s gospel still needed defending.

Around 200, Serapion, bishop of Antioch, first allowed the church at Rhossus to read the Gospel of Peter. Then he learned it could support the view that Jesus only seemed to be human, and withdrew his permission (Eusebius, Church History 6.12). Books came in and went out as teaching changed.

Codex Sinaiticus, of the fourth century, the oldest complete New Testament, includes the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas. Hermas had been among the most copied books of early Christian Egypt. In 367 Athanasius of Alexandria listed exactly our twenty-seven books, and the councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) adopted them in the West. The Council of Nicaea in 325 met over the nature of Christ, and no list of books came out of it.

Still arriving

The East doubted Revelation for centuries: Cyril of Jerusalem and Gregory of Nazianzus left it out. The Syriac Peshitta has no 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude or Revelation. Some medieval Latin Bibles carry a letter of Paul to the Laodiceans. Luther called James “an epistle of straw” and moved Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation to the back of his Bible. Churches today still count different books, as the book list shows. The New Testament was assembled slowly, by many hands, and its edges have never been fixed for everyone.

Source: after C. J. Cornthwaite, his video on how the New Testament came together. See Sources.

For the long road to a fixed list, see Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), pp. 103 and 118 to 120. See Sources.
